'''Markus Rex''' (born 28 November 1966 in [[Braunschweig]], Germany) is a German polar researcher, climate scientist, physicist, and author. His research focuses on atmospheric physics, polar climate processes, ozone depletion, and interactions between the atmosphere and sea ice. He is best known for leading the [[MOSAiC Expedition|MOSAiC expedition]] (2019–2020), the largest international Arctic research expedition to date. He is a professor at the [[University of Potsdam]] and serves as head of the Atmospheric Physics Section at the [[Alfred Wegener Institute for Polar and Marine Research|Alfred Wegener Institute]] (AWI).<ref>{{Cite web |last=Zimmermann |first=Matthias |date=2026-03-26 |title=“We have to be incredibly fast in our research”—climate researcher Markus Rex on past and upcoming expeditions |url=https://www.uni-potsdam.de/en/headlines-and-featured-stories/detail/2026-03-26-wir-muessen-wahnsinnig-schnell-in-unserer-forschung-sein-klimaforscher-markus-rex-ueber-vergangene-und-neue-expeditionen |access-date=2026-06-17 |website=www.uni-potsdam.de |language=en-GB}}</ref>

== Career ==
Markus Rex was born in [[Braunschweig]], as was his sister Gundula, to Dietrich Rex, a professor of space engineering, and Ursula Rex (née Schiller).<ref>{{cite book |chapter=Rex, Dietrich |editor-last=Habel
 |editor-first=Walter |title=Wer ist wer? Das deutsche Who's Who |edition=24th |publisher=Schmidt-Römhild |location=Lübeck |year=1985 |isbn=3-7950-2005-0 |page=1001 |language=de}}</ref> After completing his secondary education at the Raabeschule in Braunschweig in 1986, he studied physics, geophysics, and meteorology at the [[TU Braunschweig|Technical University of Braunschweig]]. He later continued his studies in [[Göttingen]] and completed his diploma thesis in 1992 using data from an Arctic research project. The thesis, titled Stratospheric Ozone Depletion Rates Derived from Ozone Sounding Data of the EASOE Campaign, marked the beginning of his research on the polar ozone hole.<ref name="TUB">{{Cite web |title=Frozen at the North Pole - Expedition to the epicentre of climate change |url=https://magazin.tu-braunschweig.de/en/m-post/frozen-at-the-north-pole-expedition-to-the-epicentre-of-climate-change/ |access-date=2026-06-17 |website=TU Braunschweig {{!}} Blogs |language=en-US}}</ref>

Rex earned his Ph.D. from the [[Free University of Berlin]] in 1997 under the supervision of Karin Labitzke and Steven Pawson.<ref name="TUB" /> His dissertation was titled ''Ozone Depletion in the Arctic Stratosphere: Results of a New Measurement Strategy (Match)'' (German: ''Der Ozonabbau in der arktischen Stratosphäre: Ergebnisse einer neuen Meßstrategie (Match)''). In 2013, he completed his habilitation at the University of Bremen with a thesis on the variability and change of the polar ozone layer and their significance within the climate system.<ref name="25years">{{cite web  |title=Festschrift der Forschungsstelle Potsdam |url=https://epic.awi.de/45829/1/AWI_Potsdam_Festschrift.pdf |publisher=Alfred-Wegener-Institut |format=PDF |access-date=2026-06-17 }}</ref> From 2001 to 2004, Rex led the BMBF-funded junior research group DYCHO (Dynamics and Chemistry of the Ozone Layer in a Changing Atmosphere), which investigated the effects of dynamical and chemical processes on the ozone layer.<ref name="25years" />

Rex worked at NASA's [[Jet Propulsion Laboratory]] (JPL) at the California Institute of Technology in the United States, at the Alfred Wegener Institute, and at the University of Canterbury in New Zealand. He also served as a lecturer at the Free University of Berlin and the [[University of Bremen]].<ref name="TUB" />

In October 2016, Rex was appointed professor at the [[University of Potsdam]] and succeeded Klaus Dethloff as head of the Alfred Wegener Institute's Atmospheric Physics Section, which had previously been known as the Section for Atmospheric Circulation and Trace Constituents.<ref name="25years" />

In 2025, Rex received the NOMIS Award for groundbreaking interdisciplinary research. The award recognized, among other achievements, his leadership of the [[MOSAiC Expedition|MOSAiC expedition]] (2019–2020), the largest international Arctic research expedition to date. He announced that the prize funding would support the development of the AI-based research project Deepcloud, which aims to improve understanding of cloud feedback processes in the polar climate system.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-10-17 |title=AWI researcher Markus Rex receives 2025 NOMIS Award |url=https://www.awi.de/en/about-us/service/press/single-view/default-f093332d1b8e53093f49cef1c69bba26.html |access-date=2026-06-17 |website=www.awi.de |language=en}}</ref>
Rex is actively involved in science communication and is the author of the ''Der Spiegel'' bestseller ''Frozen at the North Pole''.<ref name="TUB" />

== Research ==

[[File:Markus_Rex_and_Matthew_Shupe.jpg|thumb|Markus Rex (expedition leader) and [[Matthew Shupe]] (co‑leader) aboard the research icebreaker ''Polarstern'' during the MOSAiC expedition.]]

Rex's research has focused on atmospheric chemistry, Arctic [[ozone depletion]], and climate processes in polar regions. In 1997, Rex was the first author of a ''Nature'' study reporting the highest recorded chemical ozone loss in the Arctic at that time and identifying mechanisms that allowed ozone depletion to persist well into spring. The findings contributed to understanding the conditions that can lead to severe Arctic ozone loss.<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Rex | first1=Markus | last2=Harris | first2=Neil R. P. | last3=von der Gathen | first3=Peter | last4=Lehmann | first4=Ralph | last5=Braathen | first5=Geir O. | last6=Reimer | first6=Eberhard | last7=Beck | first7=Alexander | last8=Chipperfield | first8=Martyn P. | last9=Alfier | first9=Reimond | last10=Allaart | first10=Marc | last11=O'Connor | first11=Fiona | last12=Dier | first12=Horst | last13=Dorokhov | first13=Valery | last14=Fast | first14=Hans | last15=Gil | first15=Manuel | last16=Kyrö | first16=Esko | last17=Litynska | first17=Zenobia | last18=Mikkelsen | first18=Ib Steen | last19=Molyneux | first19=Mike G. | last20=Nakane | first20=Hideaki | last21=Notholt | first21=Justus | last22=Rummukainen | first22=Markku | last23=Viatte | first23=Pierre | last24=Wenger | first24=John | title=Prolonged stratospheric ozone loss in the 1995–96 Arctic winter | journal=Nature | volume=389 | issue=6653 | date=1997 | issn=0028-0836 | doi=10.1038/39849 | pages=835–838 | url=https://www.nature.com/articles/39849 | access-date=2026-06-17| url-access=subscription }}</ref> In 2004, Rex and colleagues provided the first empirical quantification of the relationship between Arctic ozone loss and stratospheric climate change, showing that cooling of the Arctic lower [[stratosphere]] substantially increases ozone depletion and suggesting that severe ozone losses observed during the 1990s resulted from both anthropogenic halogens and long-term changes in Arctic stratospheric climate.<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Rex | first1=M. | last2=Salawitch | first2=R. J. | last3=von der Gathen | first3=P. | last4=Harris | first4=N. R. P. | last5=Chipperfield | first5=M. P. | last6=Naujokat | first6=B. | title=Arctic ozone loss and climate change | journal=Geophysical Research Letters | volume=31 | issue=4 | date=2004 | issn=0094-8276 | doi=10.1029/2003GL018844 | url=https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1029/2003GL018844 | access-date=2026-06-17 }}</ref>

Rex and colleagues also developed the SWIFT (Semi-empirical Weighted Iterative Fit Technique) ozone chemistry module, a computationally efficient version of the ATLAS model designed for coupling ozone chemistry to climate models.<ref name="25years" />

In 2014, Rex and colleagues reported the discovery of a large region over the tropical western Pacific with unusually low [[Hydroxyl radical|atmospheric oxidation capacity]], suggesting a previously unrecognized pathway for the transport of [[pollutant]]s into the stratosphere.<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Rex | first1=M. | last2=Wohltmann | first2=I. | last3=Ridder | first3=T. | last4=Lehmann | first4=R. | last5=Rosenlof | first5=K. | last6=Wennberg | first6=P. | last7=Weisenstein | first7=D. | last8=Notholt | first8=J. | last9=Krüger | first9=K. | last10=Mohr | first10=V. | last11=Tegtmeier | first11=S. | title=A tropical West Pacific OH minimum and implications for stratospheric composition | journal=Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics | volume=14 | issue=9 | date=2014-05-15 | issn=1680-7324 | doi=10.5194/acp-14-4827-2014 | doi-access=free | pages=4827–4841}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Previously unknown atmospheric phenomenon discovered over tropical West Pacific |url=https://phys.org/news/2014-04-previously-unknown-atmospheric-phenomenon.html |website=Phys.org |date=29 April 2014 |access-date=2026-06-17}}</ref>

From 2019 to 2020, Rex, together with his two deputies, Klaus Dethloff and [[Matthew Shupe]], led the international research project MOSAiC (Multidisciplinary drifting Observatory for the Study of Arctic Climate), a year-long Arctic expedition that investigated the impacts of [[climate change]]. The expedition involved hundreds of scientists from numerous countries and represented the largest international Arctic research expedition to date. During the mission, the research icebreaker ''[[RV Polarstern|Polarstern]]'' drifted with Arctic sea ice for a full year to collect observations of the Arctic climate system.<ref>{{Cite web |title=For the biggest Arctic expedition ever, scientists will trap themselves in sea ice |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/graphics/2019/national/science/arctic-sea-ice-expedition-to-study-climate-change/ |access-date=2026-06-17 |website=Washington Post |language=en}}</ref>

== Awards and honors ==

* 1999 – Ernst‑Reuter‑Preis of Freie Universität Berlin for his doctoral dissertation on atmospheric physics.<ref>{{cite web |title=Ernst-Reuter-Preis 1999 – Markus Rex |url=https://www.fu-berlin.de/sites/erg/foerderaktivitaeten/ernst-reuter-preise/erp-9/index.html |website=Freie Universität Berlin |access-date=2026-06-18}}</ref>
* 2004 – Dobson Award of the International Ozone Commission (IOC) for his research on Arctic ozone depletion, including his publication “On the unexplained stratospheric ozone losses during cold Arctic Januaries”.<ref>{{cite web |title=AWI-scientist Markus Rex receives Dobson-Award |url=https://www.awi.de/en/about-us/service/press/single-view/awi-wissenschaftler-markus-rex-erhaelt-dobson-award.html |website=Alfred Wegener Institute |date=2004-06-25 |access-date=2026-06-18}}</ref>
* 2019 – Included in Nature's "Ones to Watch in 2020" list for leadership of the MOSAiC expedition.<ref>{{cite web |last=Tollefson |first=Jeff |title=Nature's 10 |url=https://www.nature.com/immersive/d41586-019-03749-0/index.html |website=Nature |access-date=2026-06-17}}</ref>
* 2022 – Arctic Circle Prize, awarded to the Alfred Wegener Institute and the MOSAiC Expedition, which was led by Markus Rex, in recognition of their contribution to advancing understanding of Arctic climate change.<ref>{{cite web |title=The Arctic Circle Prize 2022 – Alfred Wegener Institute and MOSAiC Expedition |url=https://www.arcticcircle.org/the-arctic-circle-prize |website=Arctic Circle |access-date=2026-06-18}}</ref>
* 2024 – IASC Award for Service from the International Arctic Science Committee (IASC) for his contributions to Arctic research and leadership within the MOSAiC project.<ref>{{cite web |title=IASC Medal and Award for Service Recipients |url=https://iasc.info/capacity-building/medal |website=International Arctic Science Committee |access-date=2026-06-18}}</ref>
* 2025 – NOMIS Distinguished Scientist and Scholar Award for his project *Deepcloud*, which develops new AI‑based approaches to model cloud processes and improve understanding of Arctic cloud feedbacks in a warming climate.<ref>{{cite web |title=Celebrating the 2025 NOMIS Distinguished Scientist and Scholar Award recipients |url=https://nomisfoundation.ch/celebrating-the-2025-nomis-distinguished-scientist-and-scholar-award-recipients/ |website=NOMIS Foundation |date=2025-10-16 |access-date=2026-06-18}}</ref>
